summary: Defines a set of additional values for the NAS-Port-Type RADIUS attribute. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: A server that lets you log in wants to note how you connected. This adds new choices to the list of connection types.

subtitle: Additions to RADIUS NAS-Port-Type attribute for PPP tunneling methods

tldr.problem: The RADIUS protocol had a set of predefined values for describing how a user connected to a network access server, but new connection technologies like PPP over ATM and various PPP over Ethernet variants needed to be added to the registry.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines five new values for the NAS-Port-Type attribute: PPPoA (30), PPPoEoA (31), PPPoEoE (32), PPPoEoVLAN (33), and PPPoEoQinQ (34), allowing RADIUS servers to specify these connection types.
tldr.outcome: The IANA registry for NAS-Port-Type values was extended to include these new tunneling methods, enabling broader compatibility with emerging network technologies.

today: RFC 4603 registered these NAS-Port-Type values in the IANA RADIUS types registry. Implementations that need to specify PPP tunneling methods now use these defined values.

sections.title: The NAS-Port-Type Attribute
sections.content:
RADIUS is the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service, a protocol for centralized authentication and accounting on networks. One field RADIUS uses is the NAS-Port-Type attribute, which indicates how a user connected to the network. The existing values described connection methods like dial-up, ISDN, ADSL, and others.

As network technologies evolved, vendors began implementing new connection types—particularly various PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) tunneling methods—and needed a way to identify them in RADIUS transactions. This RFC formalizes those connection types by assigning them official attribute values.
sections.plainLanguage: When you connect to a network server, it wants to know: Did you dial up? Use cable? DSL? This adds new options to that list for newer types of connections.

sections.title: The New Connection Types
sections.content:
The five new NAS-Port-Type values represent different ways to tunnel PPP traffic: PPPoA (PPP over ATM, value 30) uses ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) as the transport. PPPoEoA (value 31) and PPPoEoE (value 32) tunnel PPP over Ethernet, optionally over ATM or over another Ethernet respectively. PPPoEoVLAN (value 33) adds a VLAN (Virtual LAN) layer to the stack, and PPPoEoQinQ (value 34) uses IEEE 802.1QinQ for even more complex network segmentation.

These values were already being used by at least one vendor in deployed systems before this RFC was published, so the document was intended to formalize what was already happening in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The new values describe ways to wrap PPP traffic in different layers: through ATM, Ethernet, VLANs, or other network technologies.

sections.title: Registry Registration
sections.content:
The document serves as a formal request to IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) to register these new values in the RADIUS types registry. The allocation follows the policy in RFC 3575. Since the values were already implemented and in use, IANA had no choice but to register them retroactively to avoid confusion and ensure consistent implementations across different vendors.

This approach of codifying vendor practice is common in IETF standards work when the horse has already left the barn—registering what is already deployed prevents fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks the official authority to write these connection types into the official rulebook, since vendors had already started using them.
